newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen, BellSouth in talks - sources.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen, BellSouth in talks - sources.

text.p: German steel and engineering group Thyssen AG and BellSouth Corp of the United States are involved in intensive talks over setting up a new telecommunications venture, sources close to the talks said on Friday.

If the talks prove successful, Thyssen could emerge from its current position as an also-ran in the race to compete with monopoly Deutsche Telekom AG as a strong challenger in a market expected to be worth more than 100 billion marks ($64.2 billion) in four years.

The talks between Thyssen and BellSouth centre on relaunching an earlier plan to set up a jointly-held company that would offer comprehensive telecommunication services in Germany when markets are deregulated in 1998.

The new twist is that Thyssen and BellSouth would merge their stakes in E-Plus Mobilfunk GmbH, Germany's number three cellular phone group, into the new company and thereby give their new venture a dominant majority in E-Plus.

This would make it possible for the Thyssen-BellSouth venture to exert broad influence over E-Plus as the main technical platform on which to launch comprehensive telecoms services to both business and residential customers.
"BellSouth has decided to strengthen its activities in E-Plus considerably," an industry source close to the talks told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
"Thyssen and BellSouth are in the process of setting up a much broader relationship in telecommunications and are now engaged in intensive negotiations," the source added.
Thyssen declined official comment and no comment was immediately available from BellSouth's European offices.
Thyssen holds a 30.1 percent stake in E-Plus and BellSouth owns around 22.5 percent. The other large shareholder in the mobile phone group is German energy group Veba AG.
Veba in turn is involved in a strategic telecoms alliance with utility RWE AG and international telecoms group Cable and Wireless.
RWE recently said it had offered Thyssen around 3.5 billion marks for its stake in E-Plus, but Thyssen has denied ever receiving such an offer.
The weekly news magazine Der Spiegel, in an advance copy of a report to appear on Saturday, said Thyssen was only trying to drive up the price of its E-Plus stake before selling out.
But a source close to the talks said this was not likely.
"This is not about the share price. Thyssen does not want to sell," the source said.

There has been an ongoing difference between E-Plus shareholders about whether they could integrate the mobile phone group into their individual telecoms strategies or to keep it at arm's length as a financial asset.

E-Plus management has lobbied hard for broader cooperation among its shareholders and to put E-Plus as a brand name at the centre of a joint strategy to enter the telecoms market in competition to Deutsche Telekom.

This would save the effort of building up a new product identity in the market and would make it possible to create a telecoms network integrating E-Plus's national wireless network and the fixed wire networks of its shareholders.
The source said Thyssen and BellSouth wanted to put pressure on Veba and RWE to clarify their strategy for using E-Plus.
"They are certainly trying to put pressure on Veba and RWE to get things moving," the source said.
-- William Boston, Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097150 ($ = 1.557 German Marks)
